'''Lance Jeremy Fortnow''' (born August 15, 1963) is a [[computer scientist]] known for major results in [[Computational complexity theory|computational complexity]] and [[interactive proof systems]]. From 2019-2026, he worked as a professor in computer science at the [[Illinois Institute of Technology]]. He served as the founding dean of the College of Computing from June 2020 to June 2025.

==Biography==
Lance Fortnow received a doctorate in applied mathematics from [[MIT]] in 1989,<ref>[http://genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=65071 Lance Fortnow] at the [[Mathematics Genealogy Project]]</ref> supervised by [[Michael Sipser]]. Since graduation, he has been on the faculty of the [[University of Chicago]] (1989–1999, 2003–2007), [[Northwestern University]] (2008–2012) and the [[Georgia Institute of Technology]] (2012–2019) as chair of the [[Georgia Institute of Technology School of Computer Science|School of Computer Science]].<ref name="FortnowHired">{{cite press release | url=http://www.cc.gatech.edu/news/college-computing-hires-fortnow-anton-lead-schools | title=College of Computing Hires Fortnow, Anton to Lead Schools | publisher=[[Georgia Tech College of Computing]] | date=March 19, 2012 | accessdate=October 4, 2012 | archive-date=October 14, 2012 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121014205053/http://www.cc.gatech.edu/news/college-computing-hires-fortnow-anton-lead-schools | url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>[http://www.eecs.northwestern.edu/people/faculty/ Northwestern University Electrical Engineering and Computer Science Department Faculty]</ref> From 1999-2003 he was a Senior Research Scientist at the NEC Research Institute.<ref>[https://lance.fortnow.com/fortnow-cv.pdf]</ref>

Fortnow was the founding editor-in-chief of the journal ''ACM Transactions on Computation Theory'' in 2009.<ref>[http://toct.acm.org/ ACM Transactions on Computation Theory]</ref> He was the chair of [[ACM SIGACT]]<ref>[http://sigact.acm.org/ ACM SIGACT]</ref> and succeeded by Paul Beame. He was the chair of the IEEE Conference on Computational Complexity<ref>[http://www.computationalcomplexity.org/ IEEE Conference on Computational Complexity]</ref> from 2000 to 2006. In 2002, he began one of the first blogs devoted to [[theoretical computer science]]<ref>[http://blog.computationalcomplexity.org/ Computational Complexity weblog]</ref> and has written for it since then. Since 2007, he has had a co-blogger, [[William Gasarch]]. In September 2009, Fortnow brought mainstream attention to complexity theory when he published an article surveying the progress made in the [[P versus NP problem]] in ''[[Communications of the Association for Computing Machinery]]''.<ref>J. Markoff, [https://www.nytimes.com/2009/10/08/science/Wpolynom.html?_r=1 "Prizes Aside, the P-NP Puzzler Has Consequences"] ''The New York Times'', October 7, 2009{{subscription required}}<br>- L. Fortnow, [http://cacm.acm.org/magazines/2009/9/38904-the-status-of-the-p-versus-np-problem/fulltext "The Status of the P Versus NP Problem"], ''Communications of the ACM'' 9 (2009)</ref>

In 2026, he announced that, with approximately 160 other tenured faculty members, he had been laid off from Illinois Tech.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://blog.computationalcomplexity.org/2026/08/unexpected-unemployment.html|title=Unexpected Unemployment|first=Lance|last=Fortnow|work=Computational Complexity|date=August 12, 2026|access-date=August 12, 2026}}</ref>

==Work==
In his many publications, Fortnow has contributed important results to the field of [[Computational complexity theory|computational complexity]]. While still a graduate student at MIT, Fortnow showed that there are no perfect zero-knowledge [[Protocol (object-oriented programming)|protocols]] for [[NP-complete]] languages unless the [[polynomial hierarchy]] collapses.<ref>L. Fortnow, [http://portal.acm.org/citation.cfm?id=28418 "The complexity of perfect zero-knowledge"] in S. Micali, editor, ''Randomness and Computation'', volume 5 of ''Advances in Computing Research'', pages 327-343. JAI Press, Greenwich, 1989</ref> With Michael Sipser, he also demonstrated that relative to a specific [[oracle machine|oracle]] there exists a language in [[co-NP]] that does not have an interactive protocol.<ref>L. Fortnow and M. Sipser, [http://portal.acm.org/citation.cfm?id=49327 "Are there interactive protocols for co-NP languages?"], ''[[Information Processing Letters]]'', 28:249-251, 1988</ref>

In November 1989, Fortnow received an email from [[Noam Nisan]] showing that co-NP had multiple prover interactive proofs (MIP). With [[Carsten Lund]] and Howard Karloff, he used this result to develop an algebraic technique for the construction of interactive proof systems and prove that every language in the polynomial-time hierarchy has an interactive proof system.<ref>C. Lund, L. Fortnow, H. Karloff, and N. Nisan, [http://portal.acm.org/citation.cfm?id=146585.146605 "Algebraic methods for interactive proof systems"], ''Journal of the ACM'', '''39'''(4):859-868, 1992</ref> Their work was hardly two weeks old when [[Adi Shamir]] employed it to prove that [[IP (complexity)|IP]]=[[PSPACE]].<ref>A. Shamir, [http://portal.acm.org/citation.cfm?doid=146585.146609#references "IP = PSPACE"], ''Journal of the ACM'' '''39'''(4):869-877, 1992</ref> Quickly following up on this (January 17, 1990, less than two months after receiving Nisan's email) Fortnow, along with [[László Babai]] and Carsten Lund, proved that [[Interactive proof system#MIP|MIP]]=[[NEXP]].<ref>L. Babai, L. Fortnow, and C. Lund, [http://portal.acm.org/citation.cfm?id=1398742 "Nondeterministic exponential time has two-prover interactive protocols"], ''Computational Complexity'', '''1'''(1):3-40, 1991</ref> These algebraic techniques were expanded further by Fortnow, Babai, [[Leonid Levin]] and [[Mario Szegedy]] when they presented a new generic mechanism for checking computations.<ref>L. Babai, L. Fortnow, L. Levin, and M. Szegedy. [http://portal.acm.org/citation.cfm?id=103428 "Checking computations in polylogarithmic time"], in ''Proceedings of the 23rd ACM [[Symposium on the Theory of Computing]]'', pages 21-31. ACM, New York, 1991</ref>

Fortnow has continued to publish on a variety of topics in the field of computational complexity including [[derandomization]], [[sparse language]]s, and [[oracle machine]]s.  Fortnow has also published on [[quantum computing]], [[game theory]], [[genome sequencing]] and [[economics]].

Fortnow's work in economics includes work in game theory, optimal strategies and prediction. With Duke Whang, he has examined the classic game theory problem of the [[prisoner's dilemma]], extending the problem so that the dilemma is posed sequentially an infinite number of times. They investigated what strategies the players should take given the constraints that they draw their strategies from computationally bounded sets and introduce “grace periods” to prevent the dominance of vengeful strategies.<ref>L. Fortnow and D. Whang, [http://portal.acm.org/citation.cfm?id=195448 "Optimality and domination in repeated games with bounded players"], in ''Proceedings of the 26th ACM Symposium on the Theory of Computing'', pages 741-749. ACM, New York, 1994</ref> Fortnow also examined the [[logarithmic scale|logarithmic]] market scoring rule (LMSR) with [[market makers]]. He helped to show that LMSR pricing is [[Sharp-P-complete|#P-hard]] and proposed an approximation technique for pricing permutation markets.<ref>Y. Chen, L. Fortnow, N. Lambert, D. Pennock and J. Wortman, [http://portal.acm.org/citation.cfm?id=1386822 "Complexity of combinatorial market makers"], in ''Proceedings of the 9th ACM Conference on Electronic Commerce'', pages 190-199. ACM, New York, 2008</ref> He has also contributed to a study of the behavior of informed traders working with LMSR market makers.<ref>Y. Chen, S. Dimitrov, R. Sami, D. Reeves, D. Pennock, R. Hanson, L. Fortnow, and R. Gonen, [http://www.eecs.harvard.edu/~parkes/radcliffe09papers/PM-strategies.pdf "Gaming prediction markets: Equilibrium strategies with a market maker", ''Algorithmica'', 2009]</ref>

Fortnow has also written a science book, ''The Golden Ticket: P, NP and the Search for the Impossible'',<ref>Fortnow, Lance ''[https://press.princeton.edu/titles/9937.html The Golden Ticket: P, NP and the Search for the Impossible]''., Princeton University Press, 2013</ref> which was loosely based on an article he had written for CACM in 2009.<ref>Fortnow, Lance, [https://cacm.acm.org/magazines/2009/9/38904-the-status-of-the-p-versus-np-problem/fulltext "The Status of the P Versus NP Problem"], review article in ''Communications of the ACM'', '''52'''(9): 78-86, September 2009</ref> In his book, Fortnow provides a non-technical introduction to the P versus NP problem and its algorithmic limitations. He further describes his book and illustrates why NP problems are so important on the ''Data Skeptic podcast''.<ref>[https://dataskeptic.com/blog/episodes/2017/p-vs-np "P vs NP"], ''Data Skeptic'', 2017</ref>
